correctness.rationale: The nonnegative off-diagonal terms preserve strict positivity, and U'=U z^p a(t), where a(t)=r^T y(t) lies between the positive minimum and maximum rates. The upper bound on U' prevents a finite-time hit of U=1, and the lower bound forces U to tend to 1. Normalizing gives w'=Qw+z^p H(y), with w=y-pi and H(y)=diag(r)y-(r^T y)y zero-sum and bounded on the simplex. An irreducible finite generator has exponential semigroup decay on the zero-sum space, without reversibility; convolution with the vanishing bounded forcing gives w to zero. Thus (z^{1-p})'=(p-1)(1-z)a(t) converges to (p-1)rbar and integration gives z^p asymptotic to a positive constant times t^{-p/(p-1)}. In the Duhamel integral divided by z(t)^p, the ratio z(t-v)^p/z(t)^p tends to 1 at fixed v and is bounded for 0<=v<=t/2 by the power asymptotic. For v>=t/2, the contribution is O(exp(-gamma t/2)/z(t)^p), hence vanishes. The limit is L=integral of exp(Qv)H(pi) from zero to infinity; multiplying by Q shows QL=-H(pi) and the zero-sum normalization gives uniqueness. Rearrangement with pi_i>0 yields the claimed inverse for known Q. It also handles equal rates, when L=0 and the mass signal alone supplies the common rate. The asymptotic for z gives the log slope. The sample has L_1=1/4 and z~1/(2t), so the t^2-composition coefficient is 1/16. The frozen checker was read, not executed; it uses numerical tolerances for linear residuals and prints rather than asserts an asymptotic-error tolerance. The limits rest on the analytic proof.
